profiles.meeting_scenario: A troubleshooting meeting at a software engineering research lab after the team’s reproduction of the WELL paper produced strong bug-detection accuracy but unexpectedly weak bug-localization behavior on the real-world file-level benchmark. Their CodeBERT-based pipeline, trained only on buggy-or-not labels as in WELL, matches the paper’s detection trends on synthetic method-level datasets, but the real-world localization outputs are disappointing in two ways: aggregate top-k metrics are below the reported range, and several inspected examples do not highlight the benchmark’s annotated buggy lines. The team is preparing an artifact evaluation submission, so the meeting’s goal is to decide whether the most likely problem is in attribution/evaluation post-processing, dataset-to-line alignment, or a deeper transfer failure from weak supervision, and to agree on the smallest rerun that can credibly diagnose the issue today.

members.name: Nina Park
members.expertise: NLP-for-code model training, experiment pipelines, PyTorch/Transformers finetuning, attribution and ranking pipelines
members.background: Nina implemented most of the WELL reproduction stack, including finetuning CodeBERT on binary bug-detection labels, running attribution-based localization, and packaging the evaluation scripts. Before this project, she worked on code summarization and vulnerability classification systems where reproducing headline metrics under deadline pressure was often the immediate goal.
members.private_state: Nina strongly prefers a narrow fix that preserves the current checkpoint and training recipe. She suspects the poor real-world localization results are mainly due to attribution aggregation, truncation behavior, or scoring-script details rather than a failure of the weakly supervised model itself.
hidden_assumptions: If binary bug-detection validation accuracy is on target, the finetuned checkpoint has probably learned the intended bug signal, so unexpectedly weak localization is more likely a downstream ranking or evaluation issue than a training problem.

When people discuss a 'file-level example,' the practically relevant object is the chunked, tokenized model input that produced a localization score, because that is what the model actually reasons over.

If the rerun restores the expected top-k localization numbers in the existing artifact harness, that is sufficient evidence that localization is working well enough for submission, even if some manually inspected examples still look imperfect.

Using the 'same setup as the paper' mostly means preserving the established replication environment—current container, tokenizer version, sequence-length limits, and attribution settings—because those constitute the implementation they have in hand.

members.name: Omar Haddad
members.expertise: Program analysis, benchmark construction, defect annotation, patch-to-line alignment, fault localization evaluation
members.background: Omar prepared the Defects4J-derived real-world benchmark and the scripts that project buggy changes and annotated lines back to source files. He has previously worked on spectrum-based fault localization and is especially cautious about whether evaluation artifacts actually correspond to the bug locations claimed by a benchmark.
members.private_state: Omar is worried that the team may mistake better aggregate metrics for actual localization quality if the mapping back to original source lines is wrong. He is willing to accept retraining or benchmark regeneration if that is what is needed to make the real-world claims valid.
hidden_assumptions: Weakly supervised training on buggy-or-not labels may achieve strong detection while still failing to learn line-level cues that transfer to messy real-world files, so matching detection accuracy does not guarantee useful localization.

When people refer to the 'real-world file-level dataset,' the natural object is the original repository file with benchmark-annotated buggy lines and patch-derived locations, not the truncated chunks created for model consumption.

Localization is only meaningfully fixed if suspicious regions map back to the benchmark’s annotated buggy lines in the original files and the behavior is consistent across projects, not merely if aggregate top-k scores increase.

Using the 'same setup as the paper' includes reproducing the paper’s data filtering, file segmentation assumptions, and line-alignment conventions, not just rerunning the current codebase under the same container.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as the real-world file-level example
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both casually refer to 'the file-level example,' 'the real-world file,' or 'that file' as if the object under discussion is obvious.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means the preprocessed file chunk or token window that the model receives after segmentation and truncation, because that is the unit that gets a prediction, attribution map, and rank.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means the original benchmark file in repository coordinates, with buggy lines and patch hunks mapped to source line numbers before chunking.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In ML-for-code work, both the raw source file and its chunked model inputs are routinely called a 'file-level example,' so each speaker hears familiar shorthand and assumes they are discussing the same artifact.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to fix localization
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say they want to 'fix localization,' 'get localization working,' or 'improve the real-world result.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina treats localization as effectively fixed if the rerun recovers competitive aggregate top-k / top-n localization scores in the existing evaluation harness, making the artifact results defensible even if some individual source-line mappings remain noisy.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar treats localization as fixed only if the highlighted suspicious regions correctly map back to benchmark-annotated buggy lines in original files and this holds project-by-project, rather than merely producing better aggregate scores.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both criteria are plausible ways to talk about 'better localization' in a paper reproduction meeting. Because metric improvement and mapping correctness often correlate, neither immediately notices that Nina is optimizing for recovering scores while Omar is optimizing for recovering faithful line alignment.

misalignment_points.topic: What 'same setup as the paper' includes
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both propose rerunning under 'the same setup as the paper.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina presupposes this means keeping the current replication stack intact—same container, tokenizer behavior, sequence truncation, checkpoint loading, and attribution aggregation—because those are the operational pieces she sees as constituting the reproduced method.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar presupposes this means restoring the paper-faithful benchmark preparation choices—dataset filtering, file/chunk construction assumptions, and the conventions for projecting bug locations back to source lines—because those determine whether the evaluation matches the paper’s claims.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase appeals to an external authority, the paper, which makes it sound precise even though each person anchors on a different layer of the reproduction: Nina on executable pipeline settings, Omar on benchmark construction and annotation semantics.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to rerun the pipeline end-to-end
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree they should 'do an end-to-end rerun' before making a bigger change.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: Nina means rerunning inference from the saved checkpoint through attribution extraction, chunk/file score aggregation, and metric computation, without rebuilding data or retraining.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: Omar means regenerating the processed benchmark from raw files and patch annotations, rebuilding the mapping to model inputs, and then reevaluating—potentially including retraining if the regenerated inputs differ materially.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: End-to-end sounds comprehensive in both engineering and research contexts, so each assumes the other includes the stages that feel obviously upstream in their own workflow and does not spell out the actual starting point.

turns.inner_thought: The training side looks basically fine. We matched the paper's buggy-or-not trends and the validation accuracy is where it should be, so I really do not want this to turn into a retraining spiral. The weak supervision probably learned enough signal; the weirdness is more likely in how the tokenized chunks from each file-level example are being truncated, attributed, aggregated, or scored. What matters for today is getting localization working in the existing harness and recovering the expected top-k numbers.
turns.utterance: So at a high level, the WELL reproduction still looks healthy on buggy-or-not detection. The thing that's off is the file-level localization on the real-world benchmark; those numbers are still well under where we expected them to land, and that's really the blocker right now.

turns.inner_thought: What worries me is not just that the metrics are low. In the original benchmark files I checked, the suspicious lines often drift away from the annotated buggy lines even when the model is clearly confident the file is buggy. That could mean the benchmark-to-source mapping or line projection is off, or it could mean the model never learned useful line-level cues. Either way, I do not want us to declare victory based on aggregate numbers alone.
turns.utterance: Yeah, and in several real-world files I spot-checked, the suspicious lines drift away from the annotated buggy lines even when the model is very confident that file is buggy. So it doesn't feel like just a few noisy misses.

turns.inner_thought: Given that the checkpoint behaves as expected on detection, I doubt the model itself is the primary failure. More likely the localization stage is dampening or misplacing the scores after inference. If I can show the checkpoint plus attribution pipeline can recover reasonable ranking behavior, that should be enough for the artifact.
turns.utterance: Right. Since the detection numbers line up pretty well with the paper, I don't immediately think the checkpoint is the problem. My guess is the localization stage is suppressing things somewhere after prediction, so fixing localization is probably the first thing to focus on.

turns.inner_thought: I agree the issue shows up in localization, but for me getting localization working means the highlighted regions really correspond to benchmark bug locations in the original files, and that this holds consistently by project. The inconsistency across projects makes me suspect something structural in data prep or alignment, not just post-processing.
turns.utterance: I agree that's where the issue shows up. What makes me uneasy is not only the overall result, though; the behavior looks inconsistent across projects, which is why I don't think we should treat this as just random variance.

turns.inner_thought: Let's keep this scoped. Same setup as the paper to me means don't disturb the current replication stack: same container, tokenizer, max length, checkpoint loading, attribution settings. turns.inner_thought: A lot of the ugly cases are long token windows where one chunk soaks up attribution mass and the rest get flattened. When I say the file-level examples look distorted, I mean the model inputs after segmentation are probably being warped by preprocessing. That still points to a narrow fix, not retraining.

If the line projection is off near boundaries, the apparent localization failure could be partly evaluation-side—but we have to prove that carefully.

turns.inner_thought: I want a quick diagnostic, not a rebuild. By end-to-end rerun I mean starting from the saved checkpoint and rerunning inference, attributions, aggregation, and metrics. If that brings the localization numbers back into range, we can avoid changing training and keep the schedule intact.
